generation.hypothesis: Equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will not retain their initial high-entropy solid-solution structure during heating because atomic transport will be governed by kinetically active, non-sluggish diffusion rather than entropy stabilization. Above about 670 K, surface-energy differences should drive Au and Cu toward the surface, where they will form an increasingly unstable shell that may melt and evaporate near 970 K.
generation.material_initial_state: The starting material will be sub-10 nm, equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles synthesized by pulsed laser deposition at about 870 K on a silicon nitride membrane. The particles will initially be FCC solid solutions with multi-twinned or icosahedral structures.
generation.intervention: The nanoparticles will be heated in situ from approximately 300 to 970 K and evaluated by aberration-corrected STEM-EDS together with atomistic molecular dynamics simulations. Temperature-dependent behavior will be compared with the initial particle population and between icosahedral and truncated-octahedral particle models.
generation.conditions: Heating will occur under vacuum, with comparisons near 470, 670, 770, 870, and 970 K. The hypothesis will concern sub-10 nm nanoparticles over this experimentally accessible interval.
generation.structural_mediator: The principal mediator will be active atomic diffusion coupled to shape evolution. Surface-energy minimization should enrich low-surface-energy Au and Cu at the particle exterior, while coalescence or an elliptical-to-spherical transition should locally enhance diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Au and Cu should diffuse outward as temperature rises, producing a surface-enriched shell. Reshaping should accelerate local transport, after which the segregated shell should become susceptible to melting and evaporation. Stability will therefore be kinetically and morphologically controlled rather than guaranteed by configurational entropy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the initial state, particles of roughly 2–4 nm should progressively disappear, the size distribution should broaden, and elliptical particles should become more spherical. Au/Cu loss near 970 K should reduce characteristic particle size by approximately 20%, despite coalescence within parts of the population.
generation.baseline: The competing baseline predicts sluggish diffusion and entropy-driven thermal stabilization, with the initial composition, size distribution, and FCC morphology remaining largely preserved during heating.
generation.boundary: Substantial instability is expected above roughly 670 K and should depend on particle size and shape. The prediction is restricted to sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt particles under vacuum up to about 970 K and should not be extrapolated to bulk alloys, other atmospheres, or the full range to 1920 K.
generation.uncertainty: The onset and magnitude of segregation may vary with initial particle shape because icosahedral and truncated-octahedral geometries could provide different diffusion pathways.
